titre: Schabowski's Slip That Brought Down the Berlin Wall (1989)
accroche: On November 9, 1989, an East German spokesman answers a question he does not have a handle on, and the Berlin Wall falls that same evening.
contenu_vulgarise:
On the evening of November 9, 1989, Günter Schabowski, a member of the Politburo of the Socialist Unity Party of Germany, holds a press conference broadcast live. He is supposed to read a note announcing a loosening of the rules for travel to the West: a text drafted that afternoon, whose preparation he did not follow. A journalist in the room asks him when the measure takes effect. Schabowski hesitates, leafs through his papers, then answers: “As far as I know… it takes effect immediately, without delay.”

## A Sentence No One Had Prepared

The text that Schabowski improvises was only supposed to apply the next morning, after the arrangements at the crossing points had been negotiated. But the sentence is broadcast live, then picked up as early as 8 p.m. by West German TV news on ARD under the headline “the GDR opens its border.” Thousands of East Berliners head to the checkpoints to see whether it is true. The border guards, who have received no instructions for this eventuality, at first refuse to let anyone through, then find themselves overwhelmed by a crowd that grows as the news spreads. At 11:30 p.m., the Stasi officer in command of the Bornholmer Straße crossing, Harald Jäger, decides on his own to open the barrier rather than have his men fire on the crowd.

## A Decision No Government Made

Nothing in the East German regime's intentions planned to open the Wall that evening: the measure was meant to organize a controlled loosening, with reorganized crossing points the next day, not to end it within the hour. At the other border crossings in Berlin, officers facing the same crowd and the same absence of instructions make, that night, the same decision as Jäger: open up rather than repress. None of them received an order to do so; each made the decision alone, within minutes, with the horizon of the risk of being held responsible for a bloodbath if the crowd forced its way through.

The shift is there: the most spectacular event of the end of the Cold War in Europe was not decided by a head of state or negotiated at a table: it comes down to a poorly worded answer in front of microphones, relayed by a television network that no East German agency controlled any longer, and to mid-ranking officers who each choose, on their own, not to use force. The fall of the Wall does not erase the decades of pressure that made it possible (the Monday demonstrations in Leipzig, the mass departures to Hungary and Austria since the summer, the economic and political exhaustion of the regime) but it is a reminder that a system running out of steam can topple on a poorly chosen word rather than on the act that, in theory, would have provoked it.

citation.texte: As far as I know… it takes effect immediately, without delay.

carte.punch: A slip at a press conference brought down the Berlin Wall that very evening.
carte.idee: On November 9, 1989, Günter Schabowski mistakenly announces that a new travel rule applies “immediately, without delay.” The news spreads, thousands of Berliners crowd the checkpoints, and an isolated officer opens the border without having received the order.

quiz.question: What concretely opened the Berlin Wall on the evening of November 9, 1989?
choix: A vote of the West German Bundestag organizing reunification
An order from the East German government announcing the immediate end of the Wall
The isolated decision of a border-crossing officer facing a growing crowd
A Soviet military intervention to defuse the crisis
quiz.explication: No official order existed to open the border that evening: it is Harald Jäger, at Bornholmer Straße, who chooses on his own to let the crowd through rather than use force, not a vote of the Bundestag, not a prepared decision of the East German regime, and the USSR does not intervene.

quiz_supplementaire.question: How does the West German network ARD relay Schabowski's announcement as early as 8 p.m.?
choix: Under the headline “the GDR opens its border”
By calling the announcement a rumor to be verified
By quoting the regime's official note word for word
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The ARD television news picks up Schabowski's sentence as early as 8 p.m. under the headline “the GDR opens its border,” even though the original text was to take effect the next day.

quiz_supplementaire.question: When was the text that Schabowski improvises actually due to take effect?
choix: A week later, after a vote by the Party
The next morning, after the arrangements at the crossing points had been negotiated
It had no planned effective date
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The text was only supposed to apply the next morning, after the arrangements at the crossing points had been negotiated, not that same evening as Schabowski announced.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What happens, that same night, at the other border crossings in Berlin?
choix: Officers receive the order to imitate Harald Jäger
Officers, facing the same crowd, also choose to open up without instructions
The East German army takes control of the crossings to prevent any overflow
The crossings stay closed until the next morning, unlike Bornholmer Straße
quiz_supplementaire.explication: At the other border crossings, officers facing the same crowd and the same absence of instructions make, that night, the same decision as Jäger: open up rather than repress.
